analysis.one_liner: Restores workers' tools to sue employers for job discrimination, capping damages at $100,000.
analysis.headline: The Republican leader's alternative civil rights bill was referred to two House committees in September 1990 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After Supreme Court rulings in 1989 made it harder to win employment discrimination cases, this bill would have restored workers' ability to challenge hiring and promotion practices that disproportionately exclude people by race, sex, religion, or national origin. It would have let judges order employers to pay up to $100,000 to deter repeat violations, added expert fees to fee awards, extended civil rights protections to discrimination in carrying out contracts, and applied employment discrimination law to congressional employees for the first time. It was the Republican leader's version of the civil rights bill debated that fall, and it sat in committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face discrimination in hiring, promotion, seniority systems, or contract performance would gain a clearer path to sue. The bill would let them prove discrimination where race, sex, or another protected trait was a major contributing factor, even if other factors were also involved, and would let judges order payments of up to $100,000 to deter repeat violators. Congressional employees would gain the same discrimination protections as private-sector workers. Plaintiffs' lawyers would gain because expert witness fees would become recoverable alongside attorney fees.

how_it_helps.text: The bill defines an unlawful employment practice as one where race, color, religion, sex, or national origin was a 'major contributing factor,' even when other factors also contributed, lowering a barrier that courts had raised.

It spells out how workers can prove 'disparate impact' cases, where a seemingly neutral practice falls hardest on a protected group, and shifts the burden to the employer to show the practice is required by business necessity.

It lets a court order an employer to pay a complaining party up to $100,000 when needed to deter future violations, and lets affected workers sue immediately for temporary injunctions without waiting out the normal administrative process.

It expands the right to challenge seniority systems adopted with discriminatory purpose, adds expert fees to recoverable attorney's fees, and extends the main employment civil rights law to discrimination in the performance, breach, or termination of contracts, not just in making them.
It applies Title VII of the Civil Rights Act to Congress itself, ending the exemption of congressional employees from federal employment discrimination law.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, including private businesses, unions, employment agencies, and federal agencies, would bear the cost of new litigation exposure and potential awards of up to $100,000 per practice, plus attorney and expert fees when they lose. Employers would also have to justify any practice that produces statistical imbalances in their workforce as a business necessity. Members of Congress, as employers of congressional staff, would lose their exemption from the law.

drawbacks.text: The bill caps recovery at $100,000 for a discriminatory practice or group of practices, no matter how serious the harm, and bars punitive-style deterrence awards in disparate impact cases, limiting compensation compared to what a broader civil rights bill would allow.

It defines 'required by business necessity' so loosely that a practice merely 'significantly served' by legitimate employment goals can survive challenge, a weaker standard for workers than the one civil rights advocates sought, and it states that a statistical imbalance in the workforce alone is never enough to make a case.

It requires that all issues in cases under the law be heard and determined by a judge, taking away the option of a jury trial for discrimination claims, and it makes it harder for non-parties to challenge consent decrees that shaped their workplace.
It creates a broad carve-out for rules barring current illegal drug use or possession, letting employers enforce such rules unless they were adopted with intent to discriminate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill genuinely restores grounds for discrimination suits that courts had narrowed, and its coverage of congressional employees is a real accountability gain. But it does so with deliberate brakes: a hard $100,000 cap, a judge rather than a jury deciding every issue, a loose business-necessity standard, and no deterrence awards in disparate impact cases. Compared to the Democratic civil rights bill debated the same fall, it is a substantially weaker remedy for workers; compared to doing nothing after the 1989 court rulings, it is a real improvement. The design reflects an attempt to be veto-proof rather than maximally protective.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees on the day it was introduced, then to a civil rights subcommittee a week later, and neither panel ever acted before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 26, 1990 and referred the same day to the House Committees on Education and Labor and on Judiciary.
On October 2, 1990 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights, and the action record shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action afterward.
The bill drew no cosponsors, and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 with the bill still in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers came out ahead: they faced no new discrimination liability, no $100,000 deterrence awards, and no loosened standards for proving disparate impact. Members of Congress also benefited, since the bill's provision putting congressional employees under Title VII, ending their exemption, never went anywhere.

for.name: Rep. Robert H. Michel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 26, 1990 as the Republican alternative civil rights measure.

for.name: President George H.W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Backed this alternative approach after vetoing the broader Democratic civil rights bill in October 1990; the Michel bill tracked the administration's preferred limits, including the damage cap and consent decree provisions.

against.name: House Education and Labor and Judiciary committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it was sent to a subcommittee on October 2, 1990 and remained there until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House agenda
against.what_they_did: Championed their own broader civil rights bill that fall and did not bring the rival Republican measure to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, so no roll-call shows the split; notably, the bill was introduced by the top House Republican, and it was the Republican counter to a Democratic civil rights bill that President Bush vetoed in October 1990, making the fight cross party lines in an unusual way.

industries.note: The bill creates new grounds for workers to sue and lets judges order payments of up to $100,000 to deter repeat violations, though the cap and the judge-only trial rule limit how much employers could ever pay. Its interest in blocking or diluting the bill ran against workers who would use those remedies.

The bill applies Title VII to Congress itself, ending the exemption that keeps congressional employees outside federal employment discrimination law. Officeholders would have become subject to the same rules they impose on everyone else.
The bill adds expert fees to recoverable attorney's fees and expands the grounds for discrimination claims, increasing both the volume and the fundability of employment discrimination cases.
